projects.subject: physics
projects.title: The Runaway Truck Escape Ramp
projects.mission: A mountain highway has an escape ramp for trucks whose brakes fail. After four recent incidents, the authority is not sure whether the ramp is long enough for the new design entry speed. Investigate what controls the stopping distance, measure the energy the ramp must remove, and approve a ramp design that stops a runaway truck safely.

learningCapsule.title: Work, Energy and Forces on an Incline

sections.title: Stopping means removing kinetic energy
sections.content: A moving truck has kinetic energy K = ½mv². To bring it to rest, the opposing forces must do work equal to that energy. For a constant opposing force F acting over a distance d, the work done is W = Fd.

sections.title: Forces along an escape ramp
sections.content: On a ramp that rises at angle θ, the component of the truck's weight along the slope is mg sinθ and it opposes the upward motion. A gravel bed adds a resistive force. The total opposing force is the sum of these, and it divides by mass to give the deceleration a = F/m.

sections.title: What does speed do, and what does mass do?
sections.content: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling the speed means four times the energy. When every opposing force is proportional to the truck's weight, mass appears on both sides of the energy equation. Check carefully what that does to the stopping distance.

levels.title: Find What Controls the Stopping Distance

questions.prompt: The incident log shows four runs on the same escape ramp. Comparing the runs, which quantity should the team investigate first as the main reason a truck needed a longer stopping distance?
questions.explanation: Incidents 1 and 2 differ only in mass (4000 kg and 8000 kg) yet both stopped in 50 m. Incidents 2 and 3 differ in entry speed (20 m/s and 24 m/s) and the distance rose from 50 m to 72 m. Speed, not mass, changes the distance in this ramp model.
hints: Compare incidents 1 and 2. Only one quantity changed. What happened to the stopping distance?
Now compare incidents 2 and 3. Which quantity changed this time?

questions.prompt: A 20% increase in entry speed (20 m/s to 24 m/s) increased the stopping distance from 50 m to 72 m, which is 1.44 times longer. If the same loaded truck entered at double the speed, 40 m/s, what should happen to the stopping distance on the same ramp?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to v², and the opposing force is constant, so the stopping distance is proportional to v². A 1.2 times speed gives 1.2² = 1.44 times the distance, matching the log. Doubling the speed gives 2² = 4 times the distance.
hints: Check how 1.2 times the speed produced 1.44 times the distance.
Find the power of speed that connects those two numbers, then apply it to a doubled speed.

levels.evidenceUse: Use incident_log.csv to compare the runs before answering.
levels.simulationUse: Change entry speed and truck mass separately and watch which one changes the stopping distance.

levels.title: Measure the Energy the Ramp Must Remove

questions.prompt: The reference brake-failure case is a loaded truck entering the ramp at the speed stated in the ramp report. How much kinetic energy must the ramp remove to bring this truck to rest?
hints: Stopping the truck means removing all of its motion energy.
Use the mass and speed in the ramp report. Remember that speed is squared.

questions.prompt: Using the ramp report, find the total force that opposes the loaded truck's motion up the ramp. Include both the gravel resistance and the effect of the slope. Take g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation: Weight = 8000 × 10 = 80 000 N. Gravel resistance = 0.30 × 80 000 = 24 000 N. Slope component = 80 000 × 0.10 = 8000 N. Total = 32 000 N = 32 kN.
hints: Two different things pull the truck back. Name both.
The slope contributes a fraction of the weight equal to sin θ.
Add the two opposing forces.

questions.prompt: The opposing force is constant. How far up the ramp does the loaded truck travel before it stops?
questions.explanation: The work done by the opposing force must equal the kinetic energy: F × d = K, so d = 1 600 000 / 32 000 = 50 m. This matches incidents 1 and 2 in the log.
hints: Connect the energy removed to the work done by the opposing force.
Work = force × distance. Use your answers from the previous two questions.

levels.evidenceUse: Take the mass, slope, gravel resistance and entry speed from escape_ramp_report.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Check your force and stopping distance against the simulation readouts before submitting.

levels.title: Test the New Design Speed

questions.prompt: The ramp standard raises the entry speed that the ramp must handle. A loaded truck now enters the existing 60 m ramp at the new design speed. Which statement is correct?
options: It stops after about 50 m, safely inside the ramp.
It needs about 72 m, so it reaches the end of the ramp while still moving.
It needs about 60 m and stops exactly at the end of the ramp.
questions.answer: It needs about 72 m, so it reaches the end of the ramp while still moving.
questions.explanation: At 24 m/s the kinetic energy is ½ × 8000 × 24² = 2 304 000 J. Dividing by the 32 000 N opposing force gives 72 m, which is longer than the 60 m ramp. This agrees with incident 3.
hints: Find the new kinetic energy at the design speed.
The opposing force on this ramp has not changed.

questions.prompt: The same loaded truck enters at the design speed and travels the full 60 m of the ramp. How fast is it still moving at the end of the ramp?
questions.explanation: Energy at entry = 2 304 000 J. Work done by the opposing force over 60 m = 32 000 × 60 = 1 920 000 J. Remaining energy = 384 000 J. So ½ × 8000 × v² = 384 000, giving v² = 96 and v ≈ 9.8 m/s.
hints: Energy that is not removed by the ramp is still kinetic energy.
Subtract the work done over 60 m from the entry energy, then solve for the speed.

questions.prompt: A heavier loaded truck of 12 000 kg enters the same ramp at the same design speed. The gravel and slope forces are proportional to weight, as in the ramp report. Compared with the 8000 kg truck, what happens?
options: The stopping distance stays the same, but the ramp must absorb 1.5 times more energy.
The stopping distance becomes 1.5 times longer and the energy is 1.5 times larger.
The stopping distance becomes shorter and the energy stays the same.
Both the stopping distance and the energy stay the same.
questions.answer: The stopping distance stays the same, but the ramp must absorb 1.5 times more energy.
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass, so it is 1.5 times larger. The opposing force is also 1.5 times larger because it is proportional to weight. The ratio, and therefore the stopping distance, is unchanged.
hints: Write kinetic energy and opposing force as proportional to mass.
The stopping distance is energy divided by force.

levels.evidenceUse: Use ramp_design_standard.txt for the design speed and available ramp length.
levels.simulationUse: Set the entry speed to the design speed and confirm where the truck stops and its exit speed.

levels.title: Approve the Ramp Design

questions.prompt: The truck must stop within the available 60 m ramp length when it enters at the design speed. What is the minimum constant deceleration the ramp must provide?
hints: The truck has to lose all of its speed over a fixed distance.
Relate speed, deceleration and distance.

questions.prompt: The authority needs a design that stops the truck within 60 m but does not exceed the deceleration limit in the standard. Each design lists its slope (sin θ) and gravel resistance as a fraction of the truck's weight. Which design should be approved? Take g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation: Deceleration = g × (sin θ + resistance fraction). The first option gives 4.0 m/s², which needs 72 m and is too long. The second gives 5.5 m/s², stopping in about 52 m but exceeding the 5.2 m/s² limit. The third gives 4.5 m/s², needing 64 m. The fourth gives 5.0 m/s², which lies between 4.8 and 5.2 and stops the truck in 57.6 m.
hints: Find the deceleration each design produces from the total opposing force divided by mass.
A valid design must be at least the minimum deceleration you found and no more than the limit in the standard.

questions.prompt: The approved design decelerates trucks at 5.0 m/s² over a 60 m ramp. Which advisory should the authority post at the ramp entrance?
options: All trucks, loaded or empty, can use the ramp safely up to about 24 m/s.
Only empty trucks can use the ramp safely at 24 m/s; loaded trucks need a lower limit.
All trucks can use the ramp safely up to 30 m/s.
The ramp only works for trucks entering below 12 m/s.
questions.answer: All trucks, loaded or empty, can use the ramp safely up to about 24 m/s.
questions.explanation: The maximum entry speed from v² = 2ad is √(2 × 5.0 × 60) = √600 ≈ 24.5 m/s. Because the opposing forces scale with weight, the deceleration does not depend on mass. A 30 m/s entry would need 90 m, and 12 m/s is unnecessarily low.
hints: Use the deceleration and ramp length to find the fastest truck the ramp can stop.
Check whether truck mass appears in your result.

levels.evidenceUse: Use the deceleration limit and ramp length in ramp_design_standard.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Test each candidate slope and gravel setting in the simulation before choosing the final design.

requiredEvidence.instruction: Read every required file and use its information while solving the mission. The evidence is part of the investigation.

files.purpose: Compare mass, entry speed and stopping distance across four ramp runs.
Read the ramp model: slope, gravel resistance, truck mass, reference case and ramp length.
files.content: Escape ramp model (use g = 10 m/s²). The ramp rises 1 m for every 10 m of ramp length (sin θ = 0.10). The gravel bed is modelled as a constant resistive force equal to 0.30 times the truck's weight, acting against the motion. Loaded truck mass: 8000 kg. Reference brake-failure case: loaded truck entering at 20 m/s. Available ramp length: 60 m.

files.purpose: Read the design entry speed, the stopping requirement and the deceleration limit.
files.content: Highway design entry speed for brake-failure trucks: 24 m/s. A truck must come to rest within the 60 m ramp. To protect the driver and cargo, the truck's deceleration on the ramp must not exceed 5.2 m/s². A candidate design is described by its slope (sin θ) and its gravel resistance as a fraction of the truck's weight.

requiredSimulation.description: Interactive physics simulation of a truck entering an inclined gravel escape ramp. Controls: truck mass, entry speed, ramp slope (sin θ), gravel resistance fraction and ramp length. It displays kinetic energy, total opposing force, deceleration, stopping distance, exit speed and a stopped / overshoot status.
requiredSimulation.integrationComment: Use the simulation to separate the effect of speed from the effect of mass, to confirm the stopping distance, and to test each candidate design against the 60 m length and the deceleration limit.
